stories.headline: PyPI Brotli packages ship the Node2Shell decoder flaw
paragraphs: OpenSourceMalware reports that CVE-2026-111497 affects PyPI `Brotli` through 1.2.0. It identifies `brotlicffi` 1.2.0.1 and 1.2.0.2 as bundling the vulnerable 1.2.0 decoder; earlier releases were not checked. The post names `Brotli` 1.2.1 and `brotlicffi` 1.2.1.0 as fixes, but did not diff or fuzz `brotlicffi` sdists or pursue Python memory corruption or code execution. It says neither release notes mention the flaw and no advisory database listed either PyPI package as of the post.

stories.headline: 11th Circuit lets Florida and Georgia enforce social-media age gates
paragraphs: EFF reports that one 11th Circuit panel issued opinions letting Florida and Georgia enforce social-media age restrictions after injunctions were lifted. As EFF describes Florida H.B. 3, covered platforms must ban accounts for anyone under 14, even with parental permission, and 14- or 15-year-olds need consent. Georgia S.B. 351, EFF says, requires parental consent for users under 16 and commercially reasonable age checks. EFF says both cases may be further appealed and are likely to continue in lower courts, with practical effects depending on platform implementation.

stories.headline: Cloudflare opens a closed beta for post-quantum geo-fenced keys
paragraphs: Cloudflare says it launched a closed-beta post-quantum GeoKey Manager for the Data Localization Suite. Wrapped private keys may be distributed globally, but Cloudflare says unwrapping requires a regional root key that does not leave the selected geography, and that a request fails closed if that key is not local. The Cloudflare One path uses HPKE with hybrid ML-KEM-768 and X25519. General availability is planned for Q1 2027. The company says this design is not yet integrated with CDN certificate keys, which still use older GeoKey Manager controls.

stories.headline: Cloudflare serves cache ranges without a customer range-size setting
paragraphs: Cloudflare says Origin Range Requests is now a self-service setting on all plans and no longer requires a customer-chosen range size. For a partial request, it serves cached bytes, fetches missing coverage on internal chunk boundaries, and can attach to an in-flight download. Cloudflare reports that R2’s p99 time to first byte dropped by about half after the move; R2’s old configured range size was 64 MiB. Cloudflare also reports that a follow-up change cut tiered-cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads by about 6% week over week. Cloudflare says origin byte-range support is needed for partial origin fetches to be useful; the setting does not make an uncacheable response cacheable.

stories.headline: Court finds OPM’s employee-record disclosure to DOGE unlawful
paragraphs: EFF reports that an October 20, 2026 summary judgment found OPM violated the Privacy Act by disclosing millions of federal employee records to DOGE agents. The court found violations of inter-agency disclosure limits and record-security and confidentiality requirements. stories.headline: Canada’s C-22 lawful-access bill is awaiting the Senate
paragraphs: EFF says Bill C-22, the Lawful Access Act, has passed Canada’s House of Commons and is before the Senate. evidence.title: Introducing full transaction detection for Cloudflare WAF | Cloudflare Blog
evidence.text: Today, we are expanding our web application firewall (WAF) by adding two new capabilities: full transaction detections and response rules. Full transaction detections evaluate each HTTP request alongside its response to identify evidence of exploitation. It helps answer both "Does this request look malicious?" and "What happened when the application handled it?" Response rules can then block the origin’s response before it reaches the requester. These are valuable protections because the latest frontier models are uncovering vulnerabilities buried deep in widely used software, giving defenders clarity on what to fix — and attackers new paths to exploit. The recent php2shell vulnerability shows the stakes: a flaw in a common software component can put applications across the Internet at risk. AI agents scanning for vulnerabilities can be extremely persistent, adapting payloads using feedback, and chaining vulnerabilities, credentials, and permissions. An application's response can reveal whether an attempt worked and give an attacker information that helps them go deeper. Inspecting incoming requests remains essential for stopping recognizable attacks before they reach an application. But some threats become clear only when the request is considered alongside what the origin returns. A suspicious input followed by a response exposing sensitive information tells a different story from the same input followed by a rejection or an error. With these new capabilities, customers can use Cloudflare-managed protections or build their own policies combining request and response properties. This extends our always-on application security framework, with detection results available in Security Analytics to support investigation. Our first managed protections using this capability address the recently disclosed php2shell vulnerability. And the best part? We are making these new capabilities generally available to all Cloudflare customers, including Free plans. Request inspection is not enough Cloudflare WAF protects websites and APIs with managed rules, custom rules, and rate limiting. Managed rules provide protection for known attack techniques and vulnerabilities while custom rules let teams create their own policies using parameters such as an IP address, URL path, headers, and request body. These controls operate at the request level to stop exploits or unwanted traffic from reaching the origin. For many threats, this is the right place to act. However, treating every suspicious request as a confirmed exploit creates a difficult choice. Broad request signatures can catch more potential attacks, but they can also show “false positives”, such as matching legitimate traffic — which then breaks the applications. Deploying only rules that do not trigger false positives reduces that risk, but can leave more room for more ambiguous traffic to reach the server. The response provides the missing evidence. Cloudflare can now correlate it with the request that produced it, so detections can account for the outcome of the entire HTTP transaction. As an illustrative example, consider an application that lets users download files. An attacker manipulates the file parameter to request a private configuration file outside the permitted directory: GET /download?file=../../config/database.ini Request inspection can recognize this path traversal attempt and block it before it reaches the application. The request alone, however, cannot establish whether the application would expose the file. It might reject the request, ignore the traversal, or return an error. If the request reaches the origin, a response like this provides additional evidence: 200 OK Content-Type: text/plain [database] username=app_service password=EXAMPLE_SECRET Full transaction detection provides a missing piece: it can correlate the attempted file access with response content characteristic of a private configuration file. Configuration-like text can legitimately appear in documentation or example downloads; combining it with a traversal attempt provides stronger evidence of sensitive data exposure than either signal alone. A response rule can then replace the origin response with a Cloudflare WAF block page and HTTP 403 before it reaches the requester, effectively blocking the exploit by preventing sensitive information from reaching the attacker. Detection and mitigation are separate by design Full transaction detection extends the always-on detection framework we introduced earlier this year. Detections analyze traffic and attach metadata to the request and response, rules then decide what to do with those results. The structure of request and response in Cloudflare’s web application firewall (WAF). Separating those jobs gives customers visibility before they design a policy. Security teams can inspect detections in their own traffic, understand which endpoints and signatures are involved, and choose the response that fits their application. Similar to the approach for the request-based Attack Signature Detection , the outcome of the detections are stored in fields that can be accessed in the response custom rules or used in managed detections to block traffic. Mirroring the request detection fields, the following new fields are added to our platform: Field Description cf.waf.signature.response.confidence Confidence values associated with matching signatures cf.waf.signature.response.categories Categories associated with matching signatures cf.waf.signature.response.ref Signature reference IDs, up to 10 The first full transaction detections focus on exploit confirmation for high profile vulnerability. It correlates suspicious input with response signals that indicate an exploit may have succeeded. We will expand coverage over time by supporting other use cases, including detecting data exposure and exfiltration signals. This is important for the Internet beyond any one application: defenses can distinguish probing from evidence of impact, while detection of exposed data and services can reach customers that do not have a dedicated security team tuning every WAF rule. Create rules on the response Detecting evidence of exploitation is most useful if you can act on it in real time. Response custom rules turn full transaction detections into inline protection by blocking a matching origin response before it reaches the requester, although it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. Security teams can now combine request and response properties with detection results to decide which responses to block. When a blocking rule matches, Cloudflare replaces the origin response with a WAF block page or a custom response. Response phase controls are available in the Cloudflare dashboard at the bottom of the Security > Security Rules page, with both managed protections and custom rules. We have released both managed and custom rules to all plans, including Free plans. Over time, we will follow the same approach we use for request detections, where managed detections for free plans focus on high-profile vulnerabilities , while paying customers get a richer catalog of detections. Managed detections All customers get the protection of the full array of transaction detections through the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default ruleset, which is designed for a simple one-click deploy and simplified configurability. When a signature matches, the managed detection will block the response and return a standard WAF block page. You can edit the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default scope to run detections only on a portion of their applications, for example by excluding or restricting the detection to a specific path. Paying customers can use detection fields in custom response rules to create more tailored policies. Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default runs on every request by default. To reduce the risk of false positives, customers can restrict the scope of the mitigation to a portion of their application. Custom rules Custom response rules are designed to give customers full control of the rule logic. A useful rule can stop an administration interface from being exposed when an authentication gateway has not marked the request as internal. For example: http.request.uri.path starts_with "/admin" and not http.request.headers["x-internal-user"][0] eq "true" and http.response.code eq 200 and http.response.headers["content-type"][0] contains "text/html" This blocks only when an unauthenticated request targets `/admin` and the origin actually returns a successful HTML administration page. It does not block ordinary authentication failures, redirects, or non-administration traffic. All customers can create response rules by combining both request and response fields. All customers can create up to three custom response rules supporting Log and Block actions. The fields and functions available in response to custom rules mirrors what your plan gives you access to in request custom rules already. Creating rules on the response body is not yet available. Following the Attack Signature Detection approach, paying customers also have access to the outcome of attack detections through the cf.waf.signature.response.* fields listed above. These fields can be combined with other parameters (such as a hostname, URL path, source IP, request header) to enable protection on a single path, or limit the policy to application-specific context. We are currently rolling out the response fields to all our accounts. If you don’t have access to them yet, please contact your account team. Investigating matching requests When a managed or custom response rule logs or blocks a transaction, the event is available in Security Events. This means responders can trace any detection back to the full context of the request and the specific rule that took action. At the moment, both request-only rules and full-transaction rules are shown together in the same analytics page. In Security Events, the events generated by response rules are part of the Managed Rules or Custom Rules service. You can filter events belonging to a specific rule ID in the relative rule list section. Get started today Full transaction detection is generally available for all zones proxying traffic through Cloudflare. To verify that you’re protected, go to Security > Security Rules in the Cloudflare dashboard. If you want to customize your policy, start by reviewing full transaction detections in Security Analytics, then create the response phase policy that fits your application. evidence.title: Bringing post-quantum cryptography to geographically fenced key management | Cloudflare Blog
evidence.text: Today, Cloudflare is launching a post-quantum geographically restricted key manager in support of our Data Localization Suite (DLS) in closed beta. This new PQ GeoKey Manager is a cornerstone of Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions, making sure that a customer's decryption keys are only accessible in their chosen geography. GeoKey Manager implements this by wrapping each decryption key such that it can only be decrypted by Cloudflare servers that are located in the allowed geography. While general availability (GA) is planned for Q1 2027, today’s launch is an important milestone on our journey to support our customers’ data sovereignty goals while also migrating all Cloudflare products to post-quantum (PQ) cryptography . Governments, financial institutions, healthcare providers, and defense organizations process highly sensitive data that can remain sensitive for years or decades after it is produced. Encryption is often required to protect this data. When classical, public-key encryption is used, adversaries do not immediately need a quantum computer today to put that data at risk: they can store the ciphertext and retain them until quantum computers can break the public key cryptography protecting it — an attack strategy known as harvest now, decrypt later. For organizations with geographic requirements, resisting that threat is only half the challenge. At Cloudflare's scale, high availability requires replicating customer data across many servers across our global network. However, many data sovereignty regulations require that certain types of data be processed only within a given geographical region. We must therefore ensure the data is end-to-end encrypted such that only servers within the region have access to the plaintext. In this post, we describe the system that makes this work. The evolution of GeoKey Manager Cloudflare pioneered the concept of geo-restricted transport layer security ( TLS ) keys back in 2017 with GeoKey Manager . This gave customers control over the locations where their private TLS keys could be unwrapped on Cloudflare’s anycast network to provide stronger technical guarantees of which region their requests are decrypted into. For instance, a customer could choose to only unwrap their private keys in India. So instead of allowing decryption across Cloudflare’s entire global network, GeoKey Manager makes sure TLS signing for each customer request happens in our India network. GeoKey Manager evolved again in 2022 with ciphertext policy attribute based encryption (ABE). Instead of tying encrypted keys to a fixed set of data centers, ABE expressed geographic requirements using attributes such as country or region, like “region = European Union” or “region = Canada + United States + Mexico”. Newly authorized servers could receive matching decryption capabilities without rewrapping every customer key. That flexibility created a challenge and opportunity for the post-quantum transition. No production-ready post-quantum ABE scheme is available today, and customers do not need a large number of regions. A simpler design meets the requirement and is easier to maintain and operate. Cloudflare therefore uses hybrid ML-KEM-768 and X25519 protection with two kinds of keys, out of which ML-KEM-768 is a NIST standard that also opens doors to highly sensitive customers. A regional root key is a symmetric secret tied to one region, and an application-specific key pair is derived from it for a single service, such as Gateway or Tunnel . This protects private-key material against harvest now, decrypt later while preserving regional key-use boundaries. Global ciphertext, regional key unwrapping In its new form, GeoKey Manager is the key foundation for Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions. It controls which region protected decryption keys can be used from and when. Separate workstreams determine where tunnels terminate, where traffic is inspected, how it is routed, and where plaintext processing occurs. But all of them depend on the region where a customer’s private key can be unwrapped, because TLS traffic can only be decrypted where that key is available. During initialization, the edge key service (the component on each Cloudflare edge server that unwraps customer private keys and uses them to serve requests) verifies that it has loaded every regional root key required by its configuration. If a configured key is missing or malformed, the service does not start. After initialization, an individual request also fails closed (Cloudflare rejects it rather than risk unwrapping a key out of region) if its metadata identifies a regional root key that is not locally available. If a request for Germany was somehow trying to decrypt in Spain or France it would fail, since neither Spain nor France have the regional root key for Germany. This guarantees that a regional root key never leaves its region, no matter what. Cloudflare needs to maintain high performance while keeping our customers’ regionalized data secure at scale. This is where the next version of GeoKey Manager comes in. We are enabling fast performance while logically separating our network by using post-quantum cryptography to restrict where customers’ private keys are unwrapped. Most of our regions will be available for customers to regionalize their workflow, and there may be product specific caveats. Customers select a region and Cloudflare manages everything else needed to unwrap their private keys within the region’s boundary. How GeoKey Manager ensures that keys are only available in a region GeoKey Manager controls where wrapped private keys can be unwrapped and used on the data plane. It does not control where requests are forwarded or routed (that’s Regional Services ), where tunnels terminate, or where traffic inspection happens (also Regional Services). GeoKey Manager separates globally distributed wrapped private keys from the regional root key required to unwrap it. Quicksilver , our global configuration distribution system, distributes wrapped private keys and its metadata across our network. It does not distribute regional root keys; that happens through a separate provisioning service that stores regional root keys and delivers them only to edge servers authorized for each region. Regional root keys follow a separate, controlled path. On the data plane, a node’s regional configuration, which region a node belongs to, determines which nodes can receive which regional root keys. Defining key hierarchy and application-specific keys Every wrapped customer private key carries metadata identifying its service context, regional boundary, and epoch. The service context is the Cloudflare service that uses the key, such as Tunnel or Gateway. The regional boundary is the approved set of Cloudflare data centers where the key may be unwrapped and used, such as data centers in Germany or the European Union. The epoch identifies which generation of the regional root key the key belongs to; each rotation creates a new epoch. For example, Acme Co. might have one key for Tunnel in Germany (acme0001) and another for Gateway in Germany (acme0002). Road Runner Inc. might have one key for Tunnel in Germany (runner0001) and another for Gateway in the European Union (runner0002). Keys with the same service context, regional boundary, and epoch use the same application-specific key pair. Therefore, compromising the Tunnel-Germany application-specific private key could expose both acme0001 and runner0001, but not the Gateway keys. Compromising the Germany regional root key could affect every application-specific key derived from that root for the same epoch, including acme0001, acme0002, and runner0001. In the current architecture, the application-specific key pair is asymmetric. The public component wraps the customer's private key material, while the private component is required to unwrap it. The resulting wrapped private key is distributed with its service context ( Access , Gateway, Tunnel, Cloudflare One client ), region, and epoch. Provisioning regional root keys Creation and Provision flows for regional root keys When Cloudflare/Admin configures a region for a CF1 use case, key management service (which also derives application-specific key pairs and wraps customer private keys) creates a regional root key and associates it with a regional boundary and epoch and sends it to provisioning service for storage and distribution which under the hood uses Vault, which is managed by us on-premises. Authorizing edge servers for a region Regional root keys distribution flows Before an edge server can receive a regional root key, provisioning service evaluates three inputs: Trusted Platform Module (TPM) proves that the server possesses a registered hardware identity Zinc , Cloudflare's server inventory system, maps that identity to a data center and location Provisioning service determines which regional root keys the server may access Zinc updates its membership records for each edge server. This asynchronous process adds new servers as the network grows and removes servers when they are decommissioned. As Cloudflare performs maintenance on data centers in Germany, the definition of which data centers belong in Germany changes in Zinc. That definition is swiftly propagated through our network with Quicksilver so that our edge is up to date. The reverse also works. As we add capacity to our network, the definition of Germany, or any other region, is updated in Zinc and that is also swiftly propagated through our network with Quicksilver. Zinc also associates a registered hardware identity with a server and physical location, which supports FIPS 140-3 compliance. TPM-backed identity, server inventory data, and regional configurations determine which region an edge server belongs to and what regional root keys it can access. Each edge server calls the control plane’s provisioning service, and provides its registered hardware identity. After verifying the server’s hardware identity and regional membership, the provisioning service issues a token that permits the server to retrieve only the regional root keys authorized for its location. Each edge server receives its token and uses it to fetch the regional root keys. Authorized edge servers load regional root keys into the kernel keyring rather than persisting them on disk. Process level access controls limit which services can use them. Because this memory is volatile, a machine restart removes the keys and the server must authenticate and provision them again. This adds operational complexity in exchange for reducing persistent key material which could be an attack vector for adversaries. Wrapping private keys for global distribution When the key-management service receives a customer's private key material with a service context and regional boundary, it will use the request’s regional boundary to get the regional root key and its latest configured epoch. It will then derive the corresponding asymmetric application key pair and use its public component to wrap the private key. The result is a wrapped private key and its metadata. Quicksilver will then distribute the wrapped private key and metadata across our network. Since the wrapped key requires the specified region to decrypt, global wrapped key distribution does not grant edge servers global access to the private key because unwrapping still requires the corresponding regional root key and service context. Wrapping customer private key flow Unwrapping using application-specific keys on the data plane Unwrapping customer private key flow Why we chose this cryptographic design Symmetric roots with asymmetric key wrapping Regional root keys are 256-bit symmetric secrets. GeoKey Manager derives application-specific keys from each regional root key. For the current Cloudflare One path, the control plane’s key management service derives an application-specific Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) key pair. HPKE with hybrid post-quantum KEM The Cloudflare One path uses HPKE, as defined in RFC 9180 . Its key-encapsulation mechanism (KEM) combines ML-KEM-768 with X25519 , while HKDF -SHA-256 provides key derivation and AES-256-GCM provides authenticated encryption. Combining post-quantum and classical components preserves confidentiality as long as at least one component remains secure. Designing for rotation The validated design supports two types of key rotation: soft rotation and hard rotation. A soft rotation creates a new epoch for the regional root key while retaining controlled access to a limited number of previous regional root-key epochs — let’s say one previous generation, as an example. The customer’s new private-key material is wrapped using the latest epoch, while older wrapped private keys are still usable during the transition. This is a similar concept to when a credit card company allows you to use a previous version of your credit card for recurring payments from an authorized retailer. In this case, the number of epochs we support determine how many generations of previously wrapped private keys — credit cards — are usable. This allows customers to preserve their service uptime while they transition. A hard rotation instead rewraps affected customers’ wrapped private keys under a replacement epoch so access to the previous epoch can be removed. In this case, it would be like the credit card company not allowing you to use the previous credit card for a transaction under any circumstances. Security and availability tradeoffs Failing closed is a very intentional design choice. Failing open would mean unwrapping a customer’s private key outside its allowed region rather than rejecting the request. We never do that: if any required check fails (service context, region, epoch, etc.), the request is rejected. At startup, each edge’s key service loads every configured regional root key from its Linux kernel keyring. Missing or malformed root keys prevent the edge key service from initializing. Once running, the edge key service uses in-memory copies so that it can’t be tampered with, preventing out of region or cross-region unwrapping. In practice, an edge server serves requests for a region only once its configuration and key provisioning are complete. The trust boundary (all services that can access the regional root key) includes the key-management service, the provisioning service, and authorized edge key services because each can access regional root keys. The key-management service uses them to derive application-specific keys, the provisioning service stores and distributes them, and edge key services use locally authorized copies of them. Quicksilver remains outside this boundary because it receives only wrapped private keys and associated metadata. Operating GeoKey Manager Cloudflare’s network is constantly changing. As servers enter or leave service, Cloudflare’s fleet inventory updates regional membership. This means the list of data centers that make up a region like Spain is not static. GeoKey Manager’s provisioning layer refreshes that membership several times each day, granting or removing access to regional root keys as the network changes. This process is separate from key rotation and requires no customer action. When regional membership changes, the provisioning service immediately synchronizes the server’s Linux kernel keyring with the latest authorized regional root keys. The edge key service caches these keys in process memory until it restarts or the cache expires. It then reloads the current authorized set from the kernel keyring. What’s next: Cloudflare One integration and CDN GeoKey Manager is the basis for an improved Regional Services offering for Cloudflare One; these new capabilities will be announced in a few months. Older versions of GeoKey Manager already provide geographic controls for private keys associated with CDN certificates. We are developing a separate integration that will bring this new post-quantum GeoKey Manager described here to that existing CDN capability. We will share testing and transition details when that work is ready. Getting started If you are a current DLS customer who is regionalizing CDN traffic, you can register intent to test this feature before it’s generally available for CDN traffic here . Thank you to everyone who made this product a reality. It was a huge effort across the Data Localization Suite, Cloudflare One, and Cloudflare Research teams. evidence.title: Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning | Cloudflare Blog
evidence.text: A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left. Range requests are how large files get delivered, and caching them naively easily leads to wasted network bandwidth and wasted disk operations when running a CDN at scale. So we rebuilt how our cache handles them. For R2, Cloudflare's object storage, p99 time to first byte dropped by about half, and a follow-up improvement cut tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads by about 6%. Today, we're making that new implementation available as Origin Range Requests , a self-service feature on all plans. There's no range size to tune and no need to contact support. Turn it on with a Cache Rule , and Cloudflare handles the rest. A request for part of a file An HTTP range request asks for part of a resource instead of the whole resource. The client sends a normal GET with a Range header: GET /movie.mp4 HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com Range: bytes=1048576-2097151 If the server supports the request, it returns 206 Partial Content and identifies the returned bytes with Content-Range : HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content Content-Range: bytes 1048576-2097151/524288000 Content-Length: 1048576 Range requests are common for large objects. A video player can request bytes around a seek position instead of the whole file. A download manager can resume after an interruption. A package manager can fetch part of an artifact. A client can inspect the end of a file without downloading everything before it. The client decides whether to request a range, and Cloudflare does not change that request. Instead, Origin Range Requests changes how Cloudflare satisfies it. The range-size problem Cloudflare has supported range-request caching for years via static zone configuration. The previous implementation resembled the cache-slicing described in an nginx blog post : each client request was mapped to fixed-size ranges of the file, with the range size and file extensions configured per zone. The size of each range created a tradeoff: small ranges led to many small origin requests and memory pressure on Cloudflare from coalescing all of the requests in-memory, while large ranges caused Cloudflare to download much more data than the client requested. Updates to the range size itself would invalidate cache entries, since the size was part of the cache key. This design also meant people requesting content through our network could have unpleasant experiences accessing these files. Concurrent requests that fell inside the same range, no matter how far apart each client’s requested range was, could block each other. Our nginx-based cache also couldn’t combine range caching with concurrent streaming , a feature we built to let multiple clients read a file from cache while it's still being written. Turning both on together cut responses short, so each range had to be fully downloaded before anyone could read it, and popular files needed a separate origin fetch for every range. The extra bytes could also cross several parts of our distributed cache: from the origin to one data center, between cache tiers, and then toward the client. Every hop multiplied the waste. No value works equally well for a small seek, a sequential download, a large media file, and every origin and cache topology. Our internal cache limitations were directly exposed to customers, who should not need to understand our capabilities in-depth to have files served efficiently. Fortunately, our transition from nginx to a Pingora -based caching server created an opportunity to address the implementation problems that had forced a hard-to-use setting onto customers. Fixed-size cache chunks The fix came from something Pingora was already doing. To make it easy to resume interrupted downloads, it stores every cached file on disk in fixed-size chunks. If the cache already thinks in chunks, the range size doesn't need to be a setting at all, it can just be the chunk! For a range request, Cloudflare checks which requested bytes are already cached. It serves those bytes directly. For missing bytes, it fetches origin ranges aligned to the cache's fixed-sized-chunk boundaries, stores the result in the same chunks used for ordinary cache storage, and returns only the bytes requested by the client. For example, a request for bytes 150-250 can cause Cloudflare to fetch the aligned chunk containing those bytes. The downstream response still contains only 150-250 . This does not eliminate extra work for requests smaller than our chunk size — such a request can still require fetching the whole chunk containing it. We also are taking on the cost of more work for non-aligned ranges. The difference is that the extra work is bounded and predictable, and no longer determined by a customer-selected range size that can cause unpredictable effects on us and origins. Coordinating cached and in-flight data Parsing the Range header is straightforward. The harder problem is producing one correct response when the requested bytes are split across cached data, an origin response, and downloads already in progress. At a high level, the edge: Looks up the asset headers and range-coverage metadata. Reads whatever part of the asset it can from disk or streaming in memory. Fetches missing coverage from the origin using aligned ranges. Writes the new bytes and records the completed range in metadata. Combines the pieces and sets Content-Range and Content-Length for the client response. This is a coordinator, not a single cache lookup. One request can use a cached prefix, an in-flight download, and a newly fetched suffix. The internal origin response can be larger than the downstream response, but the downstream status and headers describe only the requested range. If an existing download covers another request's bytes, the second request can attach to that download instead of starting another origin fetch. This shares work during bursts for popular large files. The design uses the existing cache data model. Headers identify the asset version, the body is stored in bounded chunks, and metadata records which ranges were written successfully. Validate before composing Composed range responses are valid only when all bytes belong to the same representation. The coordinator checks that each origin response matches the requested range, that the total asset size is stable, and that the entity tag remains consistent across subrequests. The If-Range header lets a client request a range only if the representation still matches a known validator. If it does not match, Cloudflare returns the full representation instead of combining bytes from different versions. Cloudflare also avoids composing ranges for a representation it is about to decompress because the range over a set of compressed bytes would be different from those selected by the range in a decompressed response. In these cases, Cloudflare serves the transformed full response rather than advertising a range it cannot honor correctly. The resulting behavior is standard HTTP: A satisfiable range receives 206 Partial Content with an accurate Content-Range . An unsatisfiable range receives 416 Range Not Satisfiable . A response that cannot safely be ranged is served as the complete representation. What changed in production Before opening Origin Range Requests to everyone, we moved existing users of the old range-caching feature onto the new implementation, starting with the workloads that hurt us most. Those workloads had a lot of concurrent range requests against very large files, often on very spiky traffic. Configured range sizes on the old system ran from tens of kilobytes to tens of gigabytes. With a large range size, a request that wouldn't fill a floppy disk could make us download a few DVDs' worth of data from the origin and move it across several data centers, sometimes after the client had already given up and gone elsewhere. With a small range size, one request turned into a long line of tiny origin requests, each holding memory while it waited. Both patterns caused real operational incidents for us. R2 was the largest internal user. Its configured range size was 64 MiB, so a small read that crossed a range boundary could cost us 128 MiB of transfer between data centers. After moving R2 to the new implementation, we saw: Faster responses. Across R2's storage regions, p99 time to first byte dropped by roughly half on both cache hits and misses. Fewer bytes on our network. Our most recent change taught the coordinator to combine bytes already on disk with bytes fetched from upstream in a single response. Before, a request was served either entirely from cache or entirely from upstream. After we turned this on for R2, tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads dropped about 6% week over week, which is petabytes less data moving between our data centers every day. Getting started Once the cache no longer depended on a customer-selected range size, the product configuration could not be simpler. Customers select matching traffic through Cache Rules . Cloudflare handles the chunking and cache coordination. Origin Range Requests is intended for traffic where clients naturally request parts of a large cacheable object: Progressive and seekable video such as MP4 Resumable large downloads Software distributions and package repositories Disk images, archives, and other multi-gigabyte objects AI training and inference workloads that transfer large model files or fetch selected regions of model artifacts Clients that fetch metadata or a small region of a larger file We intend to make this the default way certain file types are served on our network, modifiable by cache rules. This feature does not change normal cache eligibility. Enabling it does not make an otherwise uncacheable response cacheable. The origin also needs to support byte ranges for partial origin fetches to be useful. To turn it on, create a Cache Rule that matches your large-file traffic and set Origin Range Requests to On. You can do this in the dashboard under Caching > Cache Rules, or through the API with origin_range_requests: { "mode": "on" } . Customers choose the traffic; the edge handles the cache coordination and correctness requirements. evidence.title: Victory! Court Rules OPM Data Disclosure to DOGE Is Unlawful | Electronic Frontier Foundation
evidence.text: In a victory for data privacy, a federal court in New York definitively ruled that the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) violated the law when it disclosed millions of federal employee records to DOGE agents. In a summary judgment ruling issued on October 20, 2026, the court found that OPM violated two provisions of the Privacy Act—one restricting disclosure of personal records between agencies and another requiring agencies to protect the security and confidentiality of records. Since the case was filed, many DOGE agents have left the government and OPM has rescinded their database access. However, OPM should still clean up the cybersecurity mess it created. The court will decide the remedy at a later date. "By virtue of the Court’s summary judgment ruling, OPM’s decision to grant DOGE Agents broad access to its systems of recordings containing [personally identifiable information (PII)] has been held unlawful," Judge Denise Cote wrote. "The record also provides no support for a finding that it was the pursuit of a modernization agenda that prompted OPM to grant sweeping and expedited access to a score of DOGE Agents to its systems of records containing PII," she added. OPM maintains databases of highly sensitive personal information about tens of millions of federal employees, retirees, and job applicants. Starting in January 2025, OPM disclosed data to the U.S. DOGE Service, initially led by Elon Musk. This disclosure violates the federal Privacy Act of 1974, a watershed anti-surveillance statute that prevents the federal government from abusing our personal information. EFF sued OPM and DOGE because this data disclosure violates the Privacy Act. We represent unions of federal employees – the American Federation of Government Employees and the Association of Administrative Law Judges – and individual employees. We seek injunctive and declaratory relief. We filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. Our co-counsel are Lex Lumina LLP , State Democracy Defenders Fund , and The Chandra Law Firm LLC . Donate to EFF Support Privacy & Government Accountability

evidence.title: Canadians Are Running Out Of Time To Oppose The Dangerous C-22 Surveillance Bill | Electronic Frontier Foundation
evidence.text: Canada’s Parliament is debating a massive expansion of surveillance powers that will threaten the privacy and security of millions of people. Bill C-22, also called the Lawful Access Act, has already passed the House of Commons, and is now before the Canadian Senate. Canadians still have an opportunity to speak out and stop this dangerous legislation. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA) is urging all Canadians to sign its petition opposing the bill. (The petition on CCLA’s website is governed by CCLA’s privacy policy.) Take action Tell the canadian senate to stop C-22 As we wrote earlier this year , Bill C-22 gives the government new powers to force digital services—including telecom companies, messaging apps, and more—to help with government surveillance. Worse, it allows Canada’s Minister of Public Safety to order companies to create a backdoor to their services for law enforcement, as long as it doesn’t lead to a “systemic insecurity.” That’s a clear recipe for weakening the encryption we all rely on. It also requires services to retain metadata for up to a year, which reveals who people communicate with, where they go, and what services they use, even when they are not suspected of any crime. Researchers at CCLA and Citizen Lab published a detailed analysis of C-22 and its serious constitutional and cybersecurity problems. The analysis points out that the bill needs more than cosmetic changes—it calls for entirely withdrawing Part 2 of Bill C-22, the section that establishes the surveillance and data retention regime. Bill C-22 could also expand the sharing of Canadians’ personal data with foreign law enforcement, including the United States. Canada has been negotiating a cross-border data-sharing agreement with the U.S. that would allow American police to get information about Canadian internet users without any Canadian court oversight. Some Canadian senators have already expressed concerns about the bill, and rightly suggested, as CCLA and Citizen Lab have, that it may not be compatible with privacy protections in the Canadian constitution. If you’re in Canada, read and sign CCLA’s petition opposing Bill C-22 today. Don’t let the Senate allow this dangerous expansion of government surveillance to become Canada’s new reality. Take action Canadians: defend your privacy and security

evidence.title: Two States Can Now Restrict Social Media Access—Here’s What To Do Next  | Electronic Frontier Foundation
evidence.text: Last week, two federal appeals courts issued opinions that will allow Florida and Georgia to start enforcing laws that will age-gate and block young people from accessing social media. The laws do not adequately respect minors’ rights to play, speak, and learn online. More fundamentally, these laws don’t help young people stay safe online—a goal that lawmakers should pursue. Age-Gated? Email EFF at agegates@eff.org . Because of the new laws, some young people will lose their ability to access lawful information, find their online communities, and even engage with school board members. Others will need parental permission to stay online. And adults will face increased demands to prove their age, which will put their privacy at increased risk simply to continue to use the services they already use. We opposed these laws because they threaten the free expression and privacy of both minors and adults. Even though these lawsuits are not over, the injunctions that paused enforcement have been lifted, and the states of Florida and Georgia will now be able to enforce broad restrictions on social media use. The restrictions that these states will start enforcing are a setback for the rights of all internet users, but they are not written in stone. That’s why EFF is encouraging internet users - and particularly young people – to start keeping a record of how they are affected. If you are a teenager who loses access to an online discussion, can’t participate in a political campaign, or stop seeking information because you don’t want to upload personal information, document what happened. The same is true for adults who may be mistakenly blocked by age checks, and parents who may encounter obstacles to authorizing their children's use of online services. These experiences matter. They can help us show courts, policymakers, and the public what government restrictions on online expression actually cost the people who live under them. Hopefully, with enough proof of the expressive harms these laws cause, we can push lawmakers to rescind them. That’s why we’re encouraging folks to reach out to EFF once they’ve documented these harms. You can write to us about this issue at the email address agegates@eff.org . The Decisions These two opinions, issued by the same panel from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit, allow Florida and Georgia to enforce restrictions on social media accounts for people under 16 years old. The requirements differ by state. In Florida , the judges allowed that state’s H.B. 3 to move forward, which requires covered platforms to ban anyone under 14 from opening or keeping accounts—even with parental permission. Teenagers who are 14 or 15 can have accounts only with parental consent. To be covered, a platform has to use algorithms, allow content uploads or the viewing of other peoples’ content, and have at least one feature on a list of features the state considers bad, including livestreaming, engagement metrics, autoplay, infinite scrolling, or push notifications. These requirements effectively apply to every major social media service that young people use. To the extent there is a silver lining in the ruling on Florida’s law, it’s that the panel recognized that H.B. 3 targets expression protected by the First Amendment. The problem is that the ruling uncritically accepts the idea that a social media service is addictive in a clinical sense, even if just 10% of users under 16 are using the platform for two or more hours per day (the standard set in H.B. 3). The court simply accepts that time spent online is a proxy for harm. The bill doesn’t distinguish doomscrolling or compulsive use from organizing a campaign, making art, or talking with friends. In Georgia , S.B. 351 can now be enforced. That law requires parental consent for anyone under 16 to hold an account on social media platforms. It also requires platforms to make “commercially reasonable efforts” to check users’ ages, which creates a hurdle for adults as well as under-16s. The ruling acknowledges that S.B. 351 “overwhelmingly applies to platforms that overwhelmingly host protected speech.” But the ruling faults the plaintiffs for not being able to show that “invalid applications substantially outweigh the valid ones.” That asks the groups challenging the law to meet a virtually impossible standard—to make their case, they would have to measure and evaluate the content hosted by all online services affected by the law. Both of these cases may be further appealed, and are likely to continue in the lower courts. But people in Georgia and Florida can no longer count on court injunctions to protect their access to the web. What the effects will be going forward depends on how platforms implement these new restrictions, including how they check ages and parental consent, as well as state officials’ views on these efforts. If you hit an age-gate while online, check out our blog post about how you might want to proceed , and our age-gating resource hub . If you want to speak out about your experience, you can talk to us at agegates@eff.org. What is Lost Some youth who lose their social media accounts will lose contact with friends. Others will lose access to a support group, the ability to speak out on current issues, or an audience for their artwork. More young people will be shut out of discussions about what’s going on in their school and their community. U.S. law has long recognized that people under 18 have their own rights to speak and receive information. These new laws interfere with those rights. The Florida opinion suggests that young people can browse the internet without an account, or use a parent’s account. But that doesn’t help those who might participate in a private group, send a personal message, or speak to an audience they have built up. Nor does it recognize the reality that in many households, young people may not have the ability to use a parent’s device, or even have healthy relationships with their parents. For parents of children under 14, the Florida law also overrides parental autonomy—even if parents wanted to allow their child on these services, they cannot do so by law. These laws won’t just harm younger kids. Adults and older teens will bear the cost of the new rules. In order to figure out who is young enough to not be able to join, or who needs parental consent to join, services will have to check users’ ages. That likely means asking people to submit ID or other sensitive information. Some people will be mis-classified as too young; others will decide that they’d simply rather stop participating instead of handing over even more personal data. Keep A Record Between the recent Meta settlement and these 11th Circuit decisions, despite widespread opposition, age-gating is becoming a reality for the American internet. As these laws are enforced, we need to understand what they mean for the people who have to deal with them. And we need to create a record of their effects on everyone’s speech so we can push to repeal them. If you encounter a restriction due to these laws that affects you, keep a record, ideally while the details are still fresh in your mind. Screenshots, along with notes about the date and time, the service involved, and the task you were trying to accomplish, will all be helpful. Did you lose an account or can’t participate? Describe what you lost. Were you using a group to organize a club, volunteer in your community, or keep in touch with friends? Did losing your account cut you off from people you wouldn’t otherwise be able to be in touch with? Even if you just used the account to access local news or follow your favorite content creator, that’s still a significant loss of your right to access information online. Record problems with age checks and parental consent. What information did the service request from you? Were you able to provide it? Did it reject your age proof, or classify you incorrectly? If you’re a parent, were you able to give permission, and what did you have to provide? What promises did the service make about what it did with the data it collected from you? Save explanations given by the platforms or any services they employ to age gate, including any law they cite. If you are to appeal a result and choose to, keep track of those attempts as well. You can also document choosing to drop out. If you abandon an account or service because you’re unwilling to provide ID or other personal data, write down what you gave up, and why. You don’t need to submit sensitive information to show that you are burdened by new rules. You Can E-Mail agegates@eff.org If these restrictions affect you, we encourage you to reach out to EFF by emailing agegated@eff.org and telling us more about what happened. EFF will continue to oppose laws that prevent adults and minors from expressing themselves online, or that push people to give up their privacy to participate in the digital world. These recent court decisions are setbacks, but they don’t settle the debate. By keeping track of people who lose access, age-check failures, and the online conversations that can no longer happen, we’ll be in a better position to challenge the worst of these restrictions, in both legislatures and courts. And in the meantime, EFF will keep fighting for laws that actually make us safer online—like stopping social media companies’ harmful surveillance of all internet users. We’ll continue to push for laws that empower parents, children, and all internet users to have meaningful choice and control over their online services. Those goals can make everyone safer online, while preserving our ability to speak and access information. Further Action Email EFF about your experience at agegates@eff.org .
