Uthmeier (Florida) EFF amicus brief in Florida case EFF amicus brief in Georgia case EFF’s Age Verification Hub

evidence.title: Python Packages Vulnerable to Node2Shell | OpenSourceMalware
evidence.text: Node2Shell ain’t just a Node.js bug: the PyPI Brotli and brotlicffi packages ship the same vulnerable C decoder. I know its been a tough week... The last week has been hell, with the PHP2Shell, LiteLLM and Railway compromises, and the Plex and GitLab security events. Oh my gosh, its been a pretty crappy week for defenders! So, I didn't get a chance to research the latest vulnerability that dropped named "Node2Shell" until today. When I read the CVE's and took a look at the Node2Shell set of vulnerabilities, I noticed that nearly all of the coverage was talking about Node.js. In fact, the handle is "Node2Shell" modelled after "PHP2Shell", but I digress! The vulnerability isn't really in Node.js at all, but instead the real issue is in Brotli. tl;dr CVE-2026-111497 (“Node2Shell”) is a vulnerability in Google’s Brotli C decoder, not in Node.js. Two Python packages on PyPI are built from that same C source: Brotli and brotlicffi . Every Brotli release up to and including 1.2.0 contains the vulnerable decoder. 1.2.1 , published 22 October 2026, is the fix and is otherwise identical to 1.2.0. brotlicffi releases up to 1.2.0.2 are affected. 1.2.1.0 , published 23 October 2026 with no release notes, is the quiet fix. Neither release mentions the vulnerability in its release notes; both packages were silently patched. If you have either installed, run pip install -U "Brotli>=1.2.1" "brotlicffi>=1.2.1.0" . As of today no advisory database lists either PyPI package, so your scanners will not tell you. What is Node2Shell? Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is a high-severity out-of-bounds write in Google’s Brotli decompression library ( c/dec/decode.c ), disclosed on 21 October 2026 by Imperva . The decoder’s DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() returns an ambiguous value when a Brotli stream requests a block-type switch that the stream never validly declared, and the fast decode path discards that return value (an unchecked-return-value flaw, CWE-252), so the decoder keeps running on corrupted internal state and writes past its ring buffer (CWE-787). Because it lives in the shared C library rather than any one runtime, it reaches everything that bundles that decoder — Node.js (where it’s reachable pre-auth through fetch() , Express 5 / body-parser request bodies, and node:zlib , earning the “Node2Shell” name), Bun, and the PyPI Brotli / brotlicffi packages — and can crash a process, leak memory, or potentially lead to remote code execution. It’s rated CVSS 4.0 9.2 (Critical) and is fixed in Brotli 1.2.1 / 1.1.1 / 1.0.10 (and Node.js 22.23.4 / 24.22.1 / 26.12.1). Back to brotli Brotli is a popular lossless compression algorithm written in C and maintained by Google on GitHub . It has 15 thousand stars, 131 contributors and is used by more than 100k other packages! Now the thing with Node2Shell is that you don't need to load or import the brotli NPM package to be vulnerable to the bug. Node bundles the C code into all versions of Node 20.x, 22.x and 24.x (before they were patched). But there absolutely is a NPM package named brotli . At OpenSourceMalware, we don't usually do software vulnerabilities. We're known for software supply chain malware research. But because I'm familiar with the library, I knew there was at least one Python package too, so I decided to take a closer look. That’s when I noticed the maintainers had quietly updated the official brotli PyPI package today. Hmmm, that's a bit suspicious! I did a comparison between version 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 and sure enough there was a difference. It turns out that there's another brotli package named brotlicffi that was also updated quietly today: I then went looking for an existing vulnerability record for the Python Brotli package in OSV, PYSEC and GHSA, and I didn’t find one. The rest of this post is what I found. "Node2Shell" Background On 21 October 2026, Node.js shipped versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1 for CVE-2026-111497, a critical-severity out-of-bounds write in its bundled Brotli decoder, reachable through fetch() , Express 5 / body-parser 2.x request bodies, and node:zlib . Imperva and others reproduced code execution against stock Node builds, and the bug picked up the name Node2Shell. What most coverage glossed over is that the vulnerable code lives in c/dec/decode.c in google/brotli . Node.js vendors a copy. So do Bun, several Linux distros, and — the subject of this post — two Python packages on PyPI (Google’s official Brotli binding and the CFFI-based brotlicffi ). The CVE record confirms this. It was assigned by Google, not by Node.js, and names github.com/google/brotli as the affected product, versions 1.0.3–1.2.0. Root cause DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() handles a “block switch”, where a Brotli stream changes which Huffman tree is used for literals, commands or distances. In the vulnerable code it returns a plain boolean: static BROTLI_INLINE BROTLI_BOOL DecodeBlockTypeAndLength( int safe, BrotliDecoderState* s, int tree_type) { brotli_reg_t max_block_type = s->num_block_types[tree_type]; ... if (max_block_type <= 1) { return BROTLI_FALSE; /* stream is invalid: a switch with only one block type */ } ... if (!SafeReadSymbol(type_tree, br, &block_type)) return BROTLI_FALSE; /* need more input */ BROTLI_FALSE means two different things here: “this stream is malformed” and “I ran out of input”. The callers can’t tell them apart, and on the fast (“unsafe”) path the return value is discarded outright: #define BROTLI_SAFE(METHOD) \ { \ if (safe) { \ if (!Safe##METHOD) { \ result = BROTLI_DECODER_NEEDS_MORE_INPUT; \ goto saveStateAndReturn; \ } \ } else { \ METHOD; \ } \ } So a stream that declares a single block type and then exhausts that block’s length forces a switch that can’t succeed. The decoder either reports “needs more input” for a stream that is complete, or carries on with the block state it had, which is where the out-of-bounds write comes from. The upstream fix, google/brotli@0ed4268 (“Detect and report invalid stream earlier”), changes the function to return a BrotliDecoderErrorCode , adds a new error BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH (−17), and replaces BROTLI_SAFE with a BROTLI_SAFE_WITH_STATUS macro at the three block-switch call sites so a format error stops decoding on both paths. The CWE pairing in the CVE record is apt: CWE-252 (unchecked return value) leading to CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). Why the PyPI packages are affected by Nodes2Shell The Brotli package on PyPI is Google’s own CPython extension. Its sdist contains the full c/ tree and compiles c/dec/decode.c into the module. Diffing the 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 sdists: $ diff -rq brotli-1.2.0 brotli-1.2.1 | grep -v PKG-INFO Files brotli-1.2.0/c/common/version.h and brotli-1.2.1/c/common/version.h differ Files brotli-1.2.0/c/dec/decode.c and brotli-1.2.1/c/dec/decode.c differ Files brotli-1.2.0/c/include/brotli/decode.h and brotli-1.2.1/c/include/brotli/decode.h differ Three files. version.h is the version bump. The decode.c and decode.h changes are commit 0ed4268, line for line. 1.2.1 is a pure security release for CVE-2026-111497, yet the release notes make no mention of the vulnerability. It was silently patched. Looking further back, the same unchecked DecodeBlockTypeAndLength → BROTLI_SAFE pattern is present in every PyPI release we checked: 1.2.0, 1.1.0, 1.0.9, 1.0.7, 0.6.0 and 0.5.2. The 0.x decoders predate the max_block_type <= 1 early return that Google’s record treats as the introduction point, but they also fail to report the invalid transition, so there is no safe older version to fall back to. brotlicffi is a separate project (the CFFI alternative used on PyPy) that vendors the same C source, so it inherits the bug. Its release history lines up with the upstream timeline: 1.2.0.1 (6 March 2026) and 1.2.0.2 (22 August 2026) bundle the vulnerable 1.2.0 decoder, and 1.2.1.0 (23 October 2026) is a quiet update published a day after the upstream fix. Like Brotli 1.2.1, its release notes make no mention of the CVE or the vulnerability; it was silently patched. We have not diffed or fuzzed the brotlicffi sdists the way we did for Brotli below. Testing To see if the Python packages were indeed susceptible to the same vulnerability, we built the Brotli 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 sdists from PyPI with AddressSanitizer and ran a crafted stream through the decoder. That gave us a single literal and distance block type, and enough commands to run the distance block counter to zero, forcing the invalid switch. We used both a C harness against each sdist’s decoder (to see the exact error code) and the Python module itself. Input Brotli 1.2.0 Brotli 1.2.1 Crafted stream, one shot consumes all ~23 MB, returns NEEDS_MORE_INPUT ERROR −17 FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH Same stream in 1-, 13-, 4096- and 65536-byte chunks NEEDS_MORE_INPUT every time ERROR −17 every time That is the vulnerable behaviour exactly as described by Imperva and in the fix commit: the decoder treats a malformed, complete stream as incomplete and keeps going with invalid state. The patched decoder rejects it before any further processing. We did not pursue the memory-corruption or code-execution side in the Python extension; the Node.js write-ups cover that, and the code is the same. Note for anyone reproducing this from Python: brotli.decompress() raises a bare brotli.error: decoder failed for any error, so you can’t see which error code fired from Python alone. A Decompressor() fed the stream incrementally will simply never finish on 1.2.0. Affected versions Brotli brotlicffi Registry PyPI PyPI Affected all releases ≤ 1.2.0 (0.5.2, 0.6.0, 1.0.1, 1.0.4, 1.0.6, 1.0.7, 1.0.8, 1.0.9, 1.1.0, 1.2.0) releases bundling the 1.2.0 decoder, including 1.2.0.1 (6 March 2026) and 1.2.0.2 (22 August 2026); earlier releases not checked Fixed 1.2.1 (22 October 2026) 1.2.1.0 (23 October 2026) Upstream google/brotli 1.0.3–1.0.9, 1.1.0, 1.2.0 → fixed in 1.0.10, 1.1.1, 1.2.1 CVE CVE-2026-111497 (CNA: Google), CVSS 4.0 9.2 In practice 1.1.0 and 1.2.0 are the Brotli versions that matter. 1.1.0 was the only release between August 2023 and October 2025, so it is what most environments have pinned. For brotlicffi , the 1.2.0.x line is the one to look for. Who is exposed on the Python side The exposure mirrors Node’s. If Brotli is importable, the common HTTP clients advertise Accept-Encoding: br and decode Brotli responses automatically: urllib3 (and therefore requests ) when Brotli or brotlicffi is installed httpx with the brotli extra aiohttp when Brotli is installed Scrapy, and anything built on the above So any Python service that fetches from servers it does not control — webhook delivery, URL previews, crawlers, SSRF-adjacent “fetch this URL” features — is handing attacker-controlled data to the vulnerable decoder. On the inbound side, any framework or middleware that decodes Content-Encoding: br request bodies is the equivalent of the Express 5 case. How to remediate pip install -U "Brotli>=1.2.1" "brotlicffi>=1.2.1.0" and rebuild any container images or wheels that bundle either. Check pip show Brotli and pip show brotlicffi in every environment; pip-audit . Tools like Dependabot and Safety will not flag this yet. If you can’t upgrade immediately, you can uninstall Brotli and brotlicffi (the HTTP clients above fall back to gzip/deflate without them) or strip br from Accept-Encoding on outbound requests and reject Content-Encoding: br on inbound ones. Advisory status As of 23 October 2026: The CVE record lists github.com/google/brotli as the affected product with commit and version ranges. It does not mention PyPI. OSV has the CVE, imported from the record, with a Git range only. A query for PyPI/Brotli 1.2.0 or PyPI/brotlicffi 1.2.0.2 returns nothing for this bug. The GitHub Advisory Database entry for the CVE lists no PyPI package. google/brotli has published no repository security advisory. We are submitting PYSEC entries to the PyPA advisory database for both packages and a PyPI package mapping to the GitHub advisory so that tooling picks this up. Until then, treat this post as the advisory. References CVE-2026-111497 record google/brotli fix commit 0ed4268 google/brotli releases 1.2.1 / 1.1.1 / 1.0.10 Node.js October 2026 security releases Imperva: Node2Shell: From Brotli Data to Remote Code Execution Aikido: Node2Shell CVE-2026-111497 OSV entry

evidence.title: The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know | Kubernetes
evidence.text:
The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know By Paco Xu (DaoCloud) | Tuesday, October 06, 2026 In Linux, cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources. Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers, ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other. With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into maintenance mode . Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25. Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy, a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation and modern resource-management features. Deprecation of cgroup v1 Kubernetes has deprecated cgroup v1 . Starting with Kubernetes v1.35, failCgroupV1 defaults to true , so the kubelet does not start on a cgroup v1 node by default. Administrators can temporarily set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration file , but removal will follow the Kubernetes deprecation policy . Further removal work is tracked in KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support . If you are still on a release older than v1.35, migrate every Linux node to cgroup v2 before upgrading, or plan to set the temporary failCgroupV1: false override. If you are already on v1.35 or later, confirm that every Linux node runs cgroup v2 (or that you intentionally keep the override). Under the default configuration, a remaining cgroup v1 node fails during kubelet startup. For kubeadm-managed clusters, Kubernetes v1.35 also makes this an earlier, stricter check. The SystemVerification preflight check, provided by k8s.io/system-validators , returns an error during kubeadm init , kubeadm join , and kubeadm upgrade when it detects cgroup v1 with kubelet v1.35 or later; with an older kubelet, the check remains a warning. See kubernetes/system-validators#1.12.1 release notes for details. The top FAQs cover three main areas: why to migrate, the benefits and drawbacks, and key points to keep in mind when using cgroup v2. Limitations of cgroup v1 and Improvements with cgroup v2 The Linux kernel documentation describes both interfaces: cgroup v1 documentation cgroup v2 documentation Let's enumerate some known issues. active_file memory is not considered available memory The kubelet treats active_file memory as not reclaimable. For I/O-intensive workloads, a large page cache can therefore make the kubelet report memory pressure and evict Pods. This is a known kubelet issue ( kubernetes/kubernetes#43916 ); migrating to cgroup v2 does not by itself change that calculation. The documented workaround is to set equal memory requests and limits for containers that perform intensive I/O, after measuring an appropriate value. Memory QoS updates in Kubernetes v1.36 Memory QoS was introduced as an alpha feature in Kubernetes v1.22 and updated in v1.27. It remains alpha in v1.36, but now separates memory throttling from memory reservation and adds tiered memory protection : Memory QoS is available only on Linux nodes that use cgroup v2. It relies on the cgroup v2 memory controller: memory.high provides throttling, while memory.min and memory.low provide hard and soft protection when tiered reservation is enabled. cgroup v1 cannot provide this protection model. Enabling the MemoryQoS feature gate applies memory.high throttling to Burstable containers. The threshold is derived from the request, limit, and memoryThrottlingFactor (default 0.9 ). memoryReservationPolicy: None is the default. It does not write memory.min or memory.low . memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation maps Guaranteed Pod memory requests to memory.min (hard protection) and Burstable Pod requests to memory.low (soft protection). BestEffort Pods receive neither protection. The kubelet exposes Alpha metrics for the total memory.min and memory.low reservations on a node. Kernel 5.9 or later is recommended. On older kernels, memory.high reclaim can trigger a known livelock; from v1.36 the kubelet logs a warning when Memory QoS is enabled on an affected kernel. For example, to opt in to tiered protection: apiVersion : kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind : KubeletConfiguration featureGates : MemoryQoS : true memoryReservationPolicy : TieredReservation memoryThrottlingFactor : 0.9 The overall Kubernetes recommendation is not to enable Alpha features in production; however, if you judge that memory QoS with tiered reservations is useful for your platform in production, make sure to test the configuration and account for hard-reserved memory before you enable the TieredReservation feature gate. See the Pod QoS documentation for the current mapping of Kubernetes QoS classes to cgroup v2 controls. Container-aware OOM handling On cgroup v2 nodes, the kubelet defaults singleProcessOOMKill to false . It therefore sets memory.oom.group for each container cgroup so that an OOM event kills all processes in that container together, rather than leaving a partially functioning multi-process container. Set singleProcessOOMKill: true only if you need the cgroup v1-compatible behavior where the kernel may kill one process at a time. See the KubeletConfiguration reference for this setting. This behavior is scoped to a container cgroup, not the whole Pod. Also, cgroup.kill is a separate administrative interface: writing 1 to it sends SIGKILL to every process in that cgroup and its descendants; it does not configure OOM behavior. The cgroup v2 memory controller additionally provides memory.events counters that monitoring systems and userspace OOM managers can observe. Rootless support In cgroup v1, delegating controllers to less privileged containers may be dangerous. Unlike cgroup v1, cgroup v2 officially supports delegation. Most implementations of rootless containers rely on systemd for delegating v2 controllers to non-root users. This delegation mechanism is separate from Kubernetes Pod user namespaces, which map container users to unprivileged host users. Pod user namespace support graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.36; check its filesystem, kernel, CRI runtime, and OCI runtime prerequisites before enabling it. What else? eBPF stories: In cgroup v1, device access controls are exposed through interface files. The cgroup v2 device controller has no interface files, and is implemented on top of cgroup BPF. Cilium attaches BPF cgroup programs for socket-based load balancing. Its default cgroup root is /run/cilium/cgroupv2 . Pressure Stall Information (PSI) reports CPU, memory, and I/O contention at node, Pod, and container level. On supported clusters, the kubelet exposes PSI by default ( KubeletPSI is stable and locked on). PSI requires cgroup v2, Linux 4.20 or later, CONFIG_PSI=y , and a kernel not booted with psi=0 . The kubelet surfaces the data through the Summary API and /metrics/cadvisor . When migrating, update software that reads the cgroup filesystem directly. The migration guidance recommends cAdvisor v0.43.0 or later and lists compatible Java, Node.js, and automaxprocs versions. CPU weight conversion in newer OCI runtimes cgroup v1 uses cpu.shares , whereas cgroup v2 uses cpu.weight . Newer OCI runtimes use an improved non-linear conversion that preserves the default priority and gives small CPU requests more usable granularity. The change is implemented in the OCI runtime rather than Kubernetes: it is available in crun v1.23 and runc v1.3.2. After upgrading a runtime, monitoring or policy tools that predict exact cpu.weight values may need updates. Read New Conversion from cgroup v1 CPU Shares to v2 CPU Weight for the formula, examples, and compatibility considerations. In-place resource updates In-place Pod vertical scaling graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.35. Kubernetes v1.36 then [enabled] (/blog/2026/04/30/kubernetes-v1-36-inplace-pod-level-resources-beta/) in-place vertical scaling for Pod-level resources by default, as a Beta feature. The kubelet coordinates changes between the Pod-level and container cgroups so that increases create headroom before container limits grow, while decreases constrain containers before shrinking the Pod-level boundary. Accurate aggregate enforcement for this v1.36 feature requires cgroup v2. Adopting cgroup version 2 Requirements Here's what you need to use cgroup v2 with Kubernetes. First up, you need to be using a version of Kubernetes with support for v2 cgroup management; that's been stable since Kubernetes v1.25 and all supported Kubernetes releases include this support. You need at least one Linux node; cgroup is a Linux-only concept Your OS install must run with cgroup v2 enabled The kernel version must be 5.8 or later (5.9 or later is recommended when using memory QoS) The container runtime must support cgroup v2. For example: containerd v1.4 or later supports cgroup v2; use containerd v2.0 or later for automatic cgroup-driver discovery CRI-O v1.20 or later The kubelet and the container runtime must both be configured to use the correct cgroup driver. See Configure the kubelet's cgroup driver to match the container runtime cgroup driver . For now, you can opt back in to use cgroup v1; the Kubernetes project recommends using cgroup v2, but in Kubernetes 1.36 (the current release) the cgroup v1 option remains supported as a fallback. That fallback is scheduled for removal in Kubernetes v1.38. If you are running an older cluster, plan to migrate; if you are setting up a new cluster with Linux nodes, you should prefer cgroup v2. In either case, review both the Kubernetes runtime documentation and (if relevant) the containerd compatibility matrix . kernel updates around cgroup v2 When Kubernetes was first announced, in 2014, only v1 cgroup existed. Version 2 cgroup management first appeared in Linux kernel 4.5, released in 2016. In Linux 4.5, the cgroup v2 io , memory , and pids controllers were supported. Linux 4.15 added support for the cgroup v2 cpu controller. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) support began with Linux 4.20. The Kubernetes project does not recommend using cgroup v2 with a Linux kernel older than 5.2 due to lack of cgroup-level task freezer support. Kubernetes documents 5.8 as the minimum kernel version for cgroup v2; the root cgroup's system-level cpu.stat file was added in Linux 5.8. The memory.high livelock fix used by Memory QoS is present in Linux 5.9 and later. memory.peak was added in Linux 5.19. cgroup driver configuration Configure the kubelet's cgroup driver to match the container runtime cgroup driver . If you use kubeadm to manage your cluster, Kubernetes recommends that you use the systemd cgroup driver, because kubeadm manages the kubelet as a systemd service. For other management tooling, check the documentation for the tool you're using to manage your cluster. If you can pick either option, I recommend using the systemd driver. Whatever tooling you've chosen, the kubelet automatically tries to detect the runtime's recommended cgroup driver. This automatic detection relies on using a runtime that implements the RuntimeConfig CRI RPC (for example: containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+). If you're using a container runtime that supports cgroup v2 but doesn't support automatic cgroup driver detection, you can manually configure an override by editing the kubelet configuration file. For example: apiVersion : kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind : KubeletConfiguration cgroupDriver : systemd Automatic discovery of the runtime's cgroup driver through the CRI, tracked by KEP-4033 , graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.34. It requires a runtime that implements the RuntimeConfig CRI RPC (containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+). When available, the kubelet uses the value reported by the runtime instead of its configured cgroupDriver value. Tools and commands for troubleshooting Tools and commands that you should know about cgroups: stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup/ : Check whether cgroup v2 is enabled; it returns cgroup2fs . systemctl list-units 'kube*' --type=slice or --type=scope : List Kubernetes-related units that systemd currently has in memory. bpftool cgroup list /sys/fs/cgroup/* : List all programs attached to the cgroup CGROUP. systemd-cgls /sys/fs/cgroup/* : Recursively show control group contents. systemd-cgtop : Show top control groups by their resource usage. tree -L 2 -d /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice : Show Pods' related cgroups directories. How to check if a Pod CPU or memory limit is successfully applied to the cgroup file? Work from the API object down to the node. Identify the node, then compare desired resources in the spec with the enacted values in status (in-place resize can leave those out of sync): kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath = '{.spec.nodeName}{"
"}' kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath = '{range .spec.containers[*]}{.name}{" spec	"}{.resources}{"
"}{end}' kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath = '{range .status.containerStatuses[*]}{.name}{" status	"}{.resources}{"
"}{end}' On that node, as root, with the systemd cgroup driver and cgroup v2 (these snippets also need jq ). Pin the container with kubelet labels; a container name alone is not unique on a node. Use crictl ps -a if the container is not running: CONTAINER_ID = $( crictl ps \ --label io.kubernetes.pod.namespace = <namespace> \ --label io.kubernetes.pod.name = <pod-name> \ --name <container-name> -q | head -n1 ) # OCI view (not the CRI protobuf field names) crictl inspect " $CONTAINER_ID " | jq '.info.runtimeSpec.linux.resources' # Kernel cgroup path for this container PID = $( crictl inspect " $CONTAINER_ID " | jq -r '.info.pid' ) CGROUP = "/sys/fs/cgroup $( awk -F: '$1=="0"{print $3}' /proc/ $PID /cgroup ) " cat " $CGROUP /cpu.weight" # request.cpu → shares → weight; not a limit cat " $CGROUP /cpu.max" # limit.cpu as "quota period"; unlimited is "max <period>" cat " $CGROUP /memory.max" # limit.memory; unlimited is "max" # Pod-level cgroup (parent slice), used by Pod-level resources cat " $( dirname " $CGROUP " ) /cpu.max" " $( dirname " $CGROUP " ) /memory.max" # Present when MemoryQoS is enabled cat " $CGROUP /memory.high" " $CGROUP /memory.min" " $CGROUP /memory.low" SCOPE = $( basename " $CGROUP " ) systemctl show " $SCOPE " \ -p CPUWeight -p CPUQuotaPerSecUSec -p CPUQuotaPeriodUSec -p MemoryMax Do not treat info.runtimeSpec.linux.cgroupsPath as a filesystem path when the runtime uses the systemd driver; that value is a systemd unit path ( slice:runtime:id ), not a directory under /sys/fs/cgroup . Expected mapping at each layer: Kubernetes: spec.containers[*].resources (desired) and status.containerStatuses[*].resources (enacted after in-place resize). Pod-level resources are on spec.resources and the parent pod slice. CRI (kubelet → runtime; these protobuf names stay cgroup v1-style even on v2): cpu_shares , cpu_quota , cpu_period , memory_limit_in_bytes , plus unified for Memory QoS. crictl inspect does not show these names; it shows the OCI spec the runtime derived from them. OCI spec: linux.resources.cpu.{shares,quota,period} , linux.resources.memory.limit , and linux.resources.unified . The runtime converts shares, quota, and period into cgroup v2 files. After upgrading crun or runc, the shares-to-weight formula may change; see CPU weight conversion . systemd scope: CPUWeight , CPUQuotaPerSecUSec , CPUQuotaPeriodUSec , MemoryMax . Unlimited or unset values often appear as [not set] or infinity. cgroupfs: cpu.weight (from CPU request; an unset request still yields the default of 2 shares), cpu.max , and memory.max on the container scope. Memory QoS adds memory.high , memory.min , and memory.low . evidence.title: Announcing Rust 1.99.1 | Rust Blog
evidence.text: Oct. 15, 2026 · The Rust Release Team The Rust team has published a new point release of Rust, 1.99.1. Rust is a programming language that is empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software. If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, getting Rust 1.99.1 is as easy as: rustup update stable If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website. What's in 1.99.1 Rust 1.99.1 fixes the following regressions from prior releases: Missing symbol wcslen : Some Rust targets were getting link errors for missing wcslen , and that function is now present in Rust's compiler-builtins library as a fallback. The LLVM loop-idiom-wcslen pass may introduce calls to wcslen as an optimization, and some Rust targets did not have that function readily available in libc or elsewhere. The UEFI targets in particular were broken for any project using std , as some of these calls were introduced in the precompiled standard library, but the issue was also reproducible for similar user code patterns. Miscompilation of FFI bool return values on x86_64 : Rust functions returning bool through FFI could leave bits 1-7 of the return register unspecified, causing callers to observe raw values other than 0 or 1 . This return type is now marked for zero-extension again, as required by the ABI. rust-lld failed to load libLLVM on macOS : This linker could fail to run if the compiler was invoked without the rustup proxy, as there was no direct setting for the appropriate library search path. Now rust-lld is built with an rpath entry for the directory containing libLLVM.dylib . If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider using the beta ( rustup default beta ) and nightly ( rustup default nightly ) channels locally and in your CI. Please report any bugs you might come across! Contributors to 1.99.1 Many people came together to create Rust 1.99.1. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks!
